summary: This article explains how sunlight is made of many colors, why tiny bits of air scatter blue light the most, and why sunsets, clouds, dusty days, and space look different.
introduce: Draw two overlapping circles on the board and quickly compare two familiar things, such as a cat and a dog, with the class. Tell students that while reading “Why the Sky Is Blue” they will look for ways things are alike and different.

keyTerms.def: the layer of air that surrounds Earth
the smallest bit of a substance, too small to see
the distance from the top of one wave to the top of the next

challengeTerms.def: the process of light being sent off in many directions when it hits small particles
a very small piece of something
a very small drop of liquid

discussion: Do you agree or disagree that anyone can explain why the sky is blue without being a scientist? Use evidence from the article to explain.
Explain why the same sky can look blue at noon and red at sunset.
struggling: Pre-teach atmosphere, molecule, and wavelength with pictures or gestures, then let weak readers fill in a T-chart of alike and different with sentence starters.
gifted: Ask strong readers to read a challenging version and write a short paragraph that uses scattering, particle, and droplet to compare two ideas from the article and explain which difference matters most.
